# Tools and code

This page describes how a workflow calls HTTP APIs and runs Python. Read [workflow-format.md](workflow-format.md) first.

Statements marked "verified in a working builder" come from a builder that created a 6-node workflow through the REST API. The workflow has code nodes, `api_call` tools, post-hooks and transitions on tool results. Its agent passed its practice cases. Statements marked "seen in a trial call" come from the event log of a simulation call made with that builder.

## Tool function shape

Every external action is a **tool function**. The shape is the same wherever you attach it.

```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 2 },
  "function": {
    "name": "lookup_order",
    "handler": "__function__:api_call",
    "description": "Look up one order. CALL it when the caller asks about a specific order.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/orders/lookup" },
        "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
        "headers": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": { "Content-Type": { "type": "string", "default": "application/json" } }
        },
        "body": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "customer_id": { "type": "string", "default": "{{customer_id}}" },
            "order_number": { "type": "string", "description": "Order number, digits only", "default": "{{order_number}}" }
          },
          "required": ["order_number"]
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.status", "variable": "order_status" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | Always `"function"` |
| `function.name` | Tool name. The model calls it by this name. Result variables are named after it |
| `function.handler` | Which runtime executes the tool. See the table below |
| `function.description` | Read by the dialogue model when the tool is in `tools`. Ignored in `pre_actions` |
| `function.parameters` | JSON-schema object. `properties` holds the parameters |
| `config.timeoutMs` | Timeout of one attempt, in milliseconds |
| `config.maxRetries` | Tool-level retries of a failed call |
| `config.interruptible` | `false` makes the tool run in the background. See "Background tools" |
| `config.alwaysRunsAt` | Makes the tool a lifecycle tool. See "Lifecycle tools" |
| `response_mapping` | Tool level, for tools in `tools`. Maps the result to variables |
| `pre_process_code` | Python hook that runs before the call |
| `post_process_code` | Python hook that runs after the call |

| Handler | Runs |
|---|---|
| `__function__:api_call` | An HTTP request |
| `__function__:code_exec` | A Python snippet in a sandbox |
| `__function__:end_call` | Hangs up. Used in the `terminal` of an `end_call` node |

Handlers for integrations, knowledge search, call transfer and rescheduling also exist. They are not needed here.

`api_call` parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `url` | Request URL. `{{var}}` works |
| `method` | HTTP method |
| `headers` | Object. Each header is a property with a `default` |
| `body` | Object. Each body field is a property under `body.properties` |
| `connect_retries` | Transport retries. See "Retries and timeouts" |

## How a parameter gets its value

One key decides, per parameter: `default`.

| Declaration | Who supplies the value | Does the model see the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `default` with a literal, or with a `{{var}}` that has a value | The workflow. The value is **baked** | No |
| `default` with a `{{var}}` that has no value when the node is entered | The model | Yes, named after the variable, with the property's `type`, `description` and `enum` |
| no `default` | The model | Yes |
| `const` | Nobody. `const` does **not** bake | It only constrains the model's own output |

Rules:

- **Use `default` for fixed backend config** such as `url`, `method` and auth headers. At registration the engine moves every `default` into the tool's base config, resolves `{{var}}` from the variable table, and removes the field from the schema the model sees.
- **Never use `const` for a value you want sent.** The engine reads only `default`. A `{{var}}` inside a `const` never resolves. An `api_call` whose `url` is a `const` fails with "URL is required".
- **Baking happens when the node is entered.** A `{{var}}` default is resolved against the variable table at that moment.

The working builder uses this for every tool: `customer_id` has `"default": "{{customer_id}}"` and is baked from a call variable. Every other body field has `"default": "{{<field name>}}"`, where no variable of that name exists, so the model fills it. Verified in a working builder.

Seen in a trial call: the model's arguments are stored as `<tool>_args.<field>` in the variable table, for example `lookup_order_args.order_number`. They were not stored under the bare field name.

Take care that a model-filled field does not share its name with a variable that is already set when the node is entered. The value would be baked and the model would never see the parameter.

### `api_call` body field rules

- Declare each body field as a leaf under `body.properties.<field>`.
- Put the field's `type`, `description` and `enum` on that leaf. Put required fields in `body.required`.
- Give each leaf its own `default`.
- Do not put a field spec at the top level of `parameters.properties` next to a `body.default` template object. The engine looks for the spec at `body.properties.<field>`, does not find it, and the model sees only "Template variable: name". The `enum` and `description` are lost while the call still works.
- A body that exists only as one `body.default` object also shows as an empty form in the dashboard editor. Saving from there removes the tool.

A `code_exec` tool is different: its parameters are true top-level arguments. Declare a model-filled one as a top-level property without `default`.

### When a baked variable has no value

| Field type | Variable unset | Variable is `""` |
|---|---|---|
| Normal field in an engine-run call (`pre_actions`, lifecycle tool) | The field is dropped from the request. No error | The field is sent empty |
| `code` of `code_exec` | The literal text `{{var}}` stays in the Python source and the snippet crashes | |

Fix: make sure an earlier node always sets the variable, even to a sentinel value. In code, read variables from `vars` and do not splice them in with `{{var}}`.

### Constrain model-filled parameters

When a value must be one of a known set, do not use a free string. The model sometimes invents a value that looks plausible.

- Use an `enum` on the leaf, and list the values in the `description` as well.
- Or use a `number` that is an index into a list, with the valid range in the description. A pre-hook or the backend turns the index into the real value.
- If neither is possible, name the exact source in the description and tell the model to copy the value unchanged.

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "queue": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Team that takes over. One of: billing, delivery, returns.",
      "enum": ["billing", "delivery", "returns"],
      "default": "{{queue}}"
    }
  },
  "required": ["queue"]
}
```

## `pre_actions` versus `tools`

The placement decides who fires the call.

| Placement | Node type | Who calls it | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pre_actions` | `api_request`, `code` | The engine | On node entry, before any model turn |
| `tools` | `conversation` | The dialogue model | During a turn, when the model decides to |
| Workflow-level `tools` with `config.alwaysRunsAt` | none | The engine | At call start or call end |

The platform removes `tools` from non-conversation nodes and `pre_actions` from conversation nodes. It does so without an error: the JSON you sent looks fine, the create call succeeds, and the stored node has an empty array. A node cannot use both.

**Use `pre_actions`** when the call must always run and the model has nothing to decide. Example: after the order number is known, always fetch the order.

**Use `tools`** when the call depends on what the user says. Example: cancel the order only if the caller asks for it.

Differences in behaviour:

| | `pre_actions` | `tools` |
|---|---|---|
| Can be skipped | No | Yes. The model may not call it if the description and the prompt do not push for it |
| Timing | Node entry | Inside a turn. The model can call a tool, speak, then call another |
| Result in the conversation | A tool call and tool result pair is added to the history | The same |
| `response_mapping` lives | On the **node** | On the **tool** |
| `description` | Ignored | The only text the model reads about the tool |

To run a fixed call before a tool-driven conversation, use a passthrough `api_request` node and transition from it into the conversation node. Do not build a long chain of passthrough nodes for optional actions. Put those into one conversation node with several tools.

### A `pre_actions` node

```json
{
  "name": "fetch_order",
  "node_type": "api_request",
  "passthrough": true,
  "passthrough_default_transition": "present",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "pre_actions": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 2 },
      "function": {
        "name": "get_order",
        "handler": "__function__:api_call",
        "description": "Get the order.",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/get_order" },
            "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
            "headers": { "type": "object", "properties": { "Content-Type": { "type": "string", "default": "application/json" } } },
            "body": { "type": "object", "properties": { "order_number": { "type": "string", "default": "{{order_number}}" } }, "required": [] }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.items", "variable": "items" }
  ],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "present", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

The last `always` transition is mandatory. A passthrough node with no matching transition deadlocks.

### Tool descriptions

In `tools`, the `description` decides whether the model calls the tool.

- Write it as an instruction with the trigger: "CALL it every time the caller gives an order number."
- A plain description such as "Looks up an order" lets the model acknowledge the request in words and never call the tool. That is the most common failure of nodes with many tools.
- If two tools could match, say which one not to use and name the other.
- In `task_message`, put the tool rules before long reference text and state: when a rule says to use a tool, call the tool.
- The working builder also tells the model to call one tool per message and to speak after every tool result. Verified in a working builder. In a trial call a model turn with no text and no tool call produced the error event "The model returned no speakable content".

A tool is available only in the nodes that list it. Seen in a trial call: the model called a tool that the current node did not list. The result was the text "The function `<name>` is not currently available."

## `response_mapping`

`response_mapping` copies values from a call result into named variables. It needs no model call.

```json
{
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.status", "variable": "order_status" },
    { "path": "data.items", "variable": "items" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | Dot path into the tool result |
| `variable` | Name of the variable to set |

### Placement

- For a tool in `tools`: inside the tool object, next to `function` and `config`.
- For `pre_actions`: at the **node level**. A `response_mapping` nested inside a `pre_actions` entry is ignored and the variable never appears.

`extraction_schema` follows the same placement rule if you use it on a call result.

### Where a result lands (trial findings)

Seen in a trial call: the result of an `api_call` is an envelope around the HTTP response.

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "data": { "ok": true, "verified": true, "attempts_left": 3 },
  "message": "Successfully executed POST request",
  "status_code": 200,
  "header": { "Content-Type": "application/json" }
}
```

`data` is the JSON body the API returned. `header` holds the HTTP response headers.

The engine also writes every result into the variable table by itself, flattened with dots. You do not need a mapping for these. For a tool named `check_answer` whose API returned `{"ok": true, "verified": true, "attempts_left": 3}`, the trial call's variable table held:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `check_answer_args.<field>` | Each argument the model sent |
| `check_answer_response.status` | `success` |
| `check_answer_response.data.ok` | `true` (a string) |
| `check_answer_response.data.verified` | `true` (a string) |
| `check_answer_response.data.attempts_left` | `3` |
| `check_answer_response.message` | `Successfully executed POST request` |
| `check_answer_response.status_code` | `200` |
| `check_answer_response.header.<Header-Name>` | One variable per response header |
| `check_answer_status_code` | `200` |
| `check_answer_success_count` | Number of successful calls so far |

Each call of the same tool overwrites the previous `_args` and `_response` values.

### Which mapping paths work

- **Start the path at the envelope, with `data.`**. If the API returns `{"ok": true}`, map `data.ok`. If it returns `{"products": [...]}`, map `data.products`. Verified in a working builder, on a tool-level mapping and on a node-level mapping.
- A path without the `data.` prefix (for the same body: `ok`) is not confirmed. A smaller example builder uses it. In an early trial call the mapped variables stayed unset and the transitions on them never fired. The mapping paths of that call are not recorded. The builder that passed uses `data.` paths.
- The flattened key can be used directly as a transition variable: `check_answer_response.data.verified`. Verified in a working builder, which tests the mapped variable and the flattened key in the same OR group as a safeguard.
- Booleans arrive as strings. The trial call showed `true` in lower case in the flattened keys. Test both `"true"` and `"True"`, or map a string field.
- A mapped list or object: the exact form it has later inside `vars` is not confirmed. The working builder reads it defensively. It accepts a list, a JSON string, and flattened keys.

## Routing on tool results

Routing runs again after a tool result arrives. A transition on a result variable fires in the same turn, before any further model turn. Seen in a trial call.

```json
{
  "transitions": [
    {
      "target_node": "load_order",
      "description": "The check passed",
      "condition": {
        "logic": "or",
        "conditions": [
          { "variable": "check_passed", "operator": "equals", "operand": "true" },
          { "variable": "check_passed", "operator": "equals", "operand": "True" },
          { "variable": "check_answer_response.data.verified", "operator": "equals", "operand": "true" },
          { "variable": "check_answer_response.data.verified", "operator": "equals", "operand": "True" }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules:

- On a passthrough node, end with an `always` transition so that a failed or empty response does not deadlock.
- Use a tool result to leave a conversation node. The pattern "a closing tool sets a variable, a transition on that variable leads to an `end_call` node" is verified in a working builder.
- To leave a node that carries out an action, do not re-test the user's earlier intent with `matches_intent`. The router looks at the latest user message and can route away before the tool was called. Extract a follow-up enum with a default such as `stay`, and branch with `equals`.

### Success and failure counters

The engine keeps two integer variables per call target. No mapping is needed.

| Placement | Variables |
|---|---|
| `pre_actions` node | `<nodeId>_success_count`, `<nodeId>_failure_count` |
| Tool in `tools` with handler `api_call` | `<toolName>_success_count`, `<toolName>_failure_count` |

Seen in a trial call: `check_answer_success_count` was `2` after two successful calls, and a code node named `setup` produced `setup_success_count` with the value `1`.

```json
{
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "give_up", "description": "The lookup failed three times", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "lookup_order_failure_count", "operator": "greater_than", "operand": 2 } ] } },
    { "target_node": "ask_again", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

### `suppress_tool_results`

A node-level boolean for nodes that run API calls. With `true` the dialogue model sees only a short `{status: "success"}` summary in place of the raw response. Variables are still mapped and routing still sees them. Use it for large responses, or when the mapped variables already hold everything the model needs.

### Background tools

A tool with `"config": {"interruptible": false}` runs in the background. A user interruption does not cancel it. Its result arrives one or more turns later. The mapped variables, the `_response` keys and the counters are filled as usual, but not in the same turn. A transition that reads them right after the call can find them unset. Gate on the variable with `is_set`.

## Retries and timeouts

| Setting | Where | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `timeoutMs` | `config` | not documented | Time limit of one attempt, in milliseconds |
| `maxRetries` | `config` | not documented | Tool-level retries after a failed response |
| `connect_retries` | `parameters.properties`, as a baked parameter | `2` | Retries when the connection could not be established |
| `timeout_ms` | `code_exec` parameter | `30000` | Time limit of a code snippet |

`connect_retries` in detail:

- It retries only failures to establish the connection: connection refused, or reset during the TCP or TLS handshake. The request never reached the server, so a repeat is safe even for POST.
- HTTP error statuses and timeouts are not retried by it.
- Hard cap `5`. `0` means a single attempt.
- Back-off is 150 ms times the attempt number, with a new connection each time.
- All attempts share one 30 second budget for the request.
- Declare it next to `url` and `method`: `"connect_retries": {"type": "number", "default": 0}`. It is not a `config` field.

The working builder sets `maxRetries` to `0` on tools that write data and to `2` on its read-only `pre_actions` call. A retried write can record the same thing twice if the API is not idempotent.

## Pre and post Python hooks

An `api_call` tool can carry two Python snippets. They run on the server, in a sandbox, right before and right after the call. They are top-level fields of the tool object.

```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 0 },
  "function": {
    "name": "check_answer",
    "handler": "__function__:api_call",
    "description": "Check one answer. CALL it every time the caller answers the question.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/check_answer" },
        "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
        "body": { "type": "object", "properties": { "answer": { "type": "string", "description": "The caller's answer", "default": "{{answer}}" } }, "required": ["answer"] }
      }
    }
  },
  "pre_process_code": "vars['member_code'] = str(vars.get('member_code') or '').strip().upper()",
  "post_process_code": "try:\n    if isinstance(result, dict):\n        result.pop('header', None)\n        d = result.get('data')\n        if isinstance(d, dict):\n            d['what_to_do_next'] = 'Ask the next question.' if d.get('verified') else 'Ask the same question again.'\nexcept Exception:\n    pass\n"
}
```

| Hook | Names available | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `pre_process_code` | `vars`: mutable dict that fills the `{{var}}` placeholders of the request. `config`: the substituted request with `url`, `method`, `headers`, `body` | Clean a value, or rewrite the whole request |
| `post_process_code` | `result`: the tool result, mutable | Reshape, shorten or extend the result |

Documented behaviour:

- The post-hook runs before `response_mapping` and extraction see the result.
- An empty or whitespace-only string means no hook.
- Hooks are honoured only on `api_call` tools (and on the integration and knowledge search handlers). The platform removes them from any other handler when the workflow is saved.
- In a pre-hook, setting `config['body']` to a string sends that string as the raw body, with no JSON encoding. Set the `Content-Type` header yourself in that case.

### What `result` looks like in a post-hook

The internal reference shows `result` as the response body. A working builder shows otherwise. Verified in a working builder:

- For an `api_call`, `result` is the envelope described above: a dict with `status`, `data`, `message`, `status_code` and `header`. The API's JSON body is `result["data"]`.
- A key that the hook adds inside `result["data"]` reaches the dialogue model as part of the tool result. The working builder adds a `what_to_do_next` sentence there, and its prompt tells the model to obey it.
- `result.pop("header", None)` removes the response headers. The working builder does this on every tool, so that headers do not take up space in the model's context.
- Mapping paths still start with `data.` when a post-hook is present.

The working builder writes every hook inside `try` and `except Exception: pass` and checks types with `isinstance` before use. What the platform does when a hook raises is not documented.

Seen in a test on 10 October: a post-hook can read call variables and write new variables, and a later pre-hook reads them. Not confirmed: whether a change to `result` also changes the flattened `<tool>_response.*` variables.

## Code nodes and `code_exec`

A `code` node runs a Python snippet when it is entered. The snippet is a `code_exec` function in `pre_actions`.

```json
{
  "name": "compute_delivery",
  "node_type": "code",
  "passthrough": true,
  "passthrough_default_transition": "tell_delivery",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "pre_actions": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "code_exec",
        "handler": "__function__:code_exec",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "code": { "type": "string", "default": "import datetime\ntry:\n    start = datetime.date.fromisoformat(str(vars.get('shipped_on'))[:10])\n    eta = start + datetime.timedelta(days=3)\n    vars['delivery_day'] = eta.isoformat()\n    vars['delivery_state'] = 'known'\nexcept Exception:\n    vars['delivery_day'] = ''\n    vars['delivery_state'] = 'unknown'\n" },
            "timeout_ms": { "type": "number", "default": 10000 }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "tell_delivery", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `code` | The Python source, as a baked `default` string |
| `timeout_ms` | Time limit in milliseconds. Default `30000` |

### Reading and writing variables

- The snippet gets a dict named `vars`. It holds the current workflow variables.
- Read with `vars.get("name")`. A variable that was never set is absent.
- Write with `vars["name"] = value`. Every key the snippet assigns becomes a workflow variable.

Verified in a working builder:

- Call variables are in `vars`. The builder reads `vars.get("now")`, a call variable passed with the simulation.
- The result of an earlier `api_request` node is reachable from `vars` in a later code node. The builder looks for it under the mapped variable name first and under the flattened result keys second. Which of the two held the data is not recorded.
- A string written to `vars["date_facts"]` in a code node resolves as `{{date_facts}}` in the `task_message` of later conversation nodes. Multi-line strings work.
- The standard modules `json`, `re` and `datetime` can be imported.
- The same snippet can run in two code nodes at different points of the call. The later run sees the variables added in between.

### What a code node returns

Seen in a trial call: the result of a successful `code_exec` is

```json
{ "status": "success", "data": null, "message": "Code executed successfully", "status_code": 200 }
```

The snippet's output is not in `data`. Its values reach the workflow only through `vars`. After a code node named `setup` ran, the variable table held:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| each key the snippet wrote, for example `date_facts` | the value, with source `tool_result` and source node `setup` |
| `setup_response.status` | `success` |
| `setup_response.data` | `null` |
| `setup_response.message` | `Code executed successfully` |
| `setup_response.status_code` | `200` |
| `setup_status_code` | `200` |
| `setup_success_count` | `1` |

For a code node the automatic keys are named after the **node**, not after `code_exec`.

### Rules for snippets

- **Do not write `{{` or `}}` in the code.** The internal sources disagree on whether the `code` field is templated. One says it is exempt. Another says placeholders are resolved when the code runs and an unset one is left as literal text, which breaks the Python. The working builder removes every `{{` and `}}` from generated code (a nested dict literal such as `{'a': {'b': 1}}` ends in `}}`) and reads all values from `vars`.
- **Never let a snippet raise.** Wrap the body in `try` and `except`, and write a fallback value for every variable that a later prompt or condition reads. A prompt that references an unset variable shows the literal placeholder to the model.
- **Write strings for routing flags**, such as `known` and `unknown`. Do not route on a Python boolean. See "Do not route on a boolean" in workflow-format.md.
- Keep snippets fast. They block the conversation.
- Do arithmetic, date calculation and counting in code, and give the model the finished facts as text. Verified in a working builder: it computes a block of date facts in a code node and places it in the prompts.
- Treat a code node like an API node: `passthrough: true`, a `passthrough_default_transition`, and a last `always` transition.

### Sandbox limits

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Time | `timeout_ms`, default `30000` |
| Modules | `json`, `re` and `datetime` are verified in a working builder. The full list is not documented |
| Network and file access | Not documented |
| Memory and output size | Not documented |

### `code_exec` as a tool

`code_exec` can also be a tool in the `tools` array of a conversation node, called by the model. Its parameters are top-level arguments, declared without `default` so the model fills them. For such a tool the `code` field resolves `{{var}}` when the tool is called, against the current variable table. The working builder does not use this form, so nothing about it is verified here.

## Lifecycle tools

A tool whose `config.alwaysRunsAt` is a non-empty list is never shown to the model. The engine fires it at a fixed point of the call.

| Value | When |
|---|---|
| `start_of_call` | During call setup, before the first turn |
| `end_of_call` | After the call has ended |
| `each_turn` | Accepted by the schema but not implemented. It never fires |

Put a lifecycle tool that must run on every call into the workflow's top-level `tools` array.

```json
{
  "initial_node": "greeting",
  "nodes": {},
  "tools": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "config": { "alwaysRunsAt": ["end_of_call"] },
      "function": {
        "name": "push_call_result",
        "handler": "__function__:api_call",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/call-results" },
            "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
            "body": {
              "type": "object",
              "properties": {
                "summary": { "type": "string", "default": "{{call.analysis.summary}}" },
                "reason": { "type": "string", "default": "{{call.call_end_reason}}" }
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules:

- A workflow-level tool without `alwaysRunsAt` never runs and the model never sees it.
- A lifecycle tool in a node's `tools` runs for `start_of_call` only on the `initial_node`, and for `end_of_call` only on the node in which the call ended.
- If a `{{var}}` parameter is still unresolved, one model call fills the parameters. If everything resolves, the handler runs directly.
- `response_mapping` is applied for `start_of_call`. It is not applied for `end_of_call`.
- At the end of a call the order is: call analysis, then `end_of_call` tools, then success-criteria judging. An `end_of_call` tool can use `{{call.analysis.summary}}`, `{{call.analysis.structured_data_str}}`, `{{call.call_end_reason}}`, `{{call.call_end_reason_category}}`, `{{call.call_tags}}` and `{{call.duration}}`.
- A malformed lifecycle tool is dropped at run time without an error. Validate with a dry run (api.md).

## Tool results and the next turn

After a tool call returns, the model sees the result and has to produce the next turn itself. Two things were seen in practice runs with the hackathon's agent model:

- **The agent says nothing after the tool call.** The result arrives, no assistant message follows, and the simulated customer hangs up after waiting. It happens more often when the result is bare data such as `{"ok": true, "verified": true}`.
- **The agent ignores a negative result.** For example it reads `"verified": false` and moves on to the next question as if the answer had passed.

What fixed both in a working builder (verified, see the post-hook section above): a post-hook on the tool that adds one plain instruction line to the result before the model sees it, for example a `what_to_do_next` field that says what the answer means and what to say or call next. The model then has something to act on.

Also say it in the step's prompt: after every tool result, speak to the customer or call the next tool. Never end a turn with nothing.

## Checklist

- Fixed values use `default`, never `const`.
- Each `api_call` body field is a leaf under `body.properties` with its own `default`, `description` and `enum`.
- `tools` only on `conversation` nodes. `pre_actions` only on `api_request` and `code` nodes.
- `response_mapping` on the tool for `tools`, on the node for `pre_actions`.
- Mapping paths start with `data.`.
- Booleans from results are tested as `"true"` and `"True"`, or replaced by string fields.
- Every passthrough node ends with an `always` transition.
- Code reads and writes through `vars`, never raises, and contains no `{{` or `}}`.
- Tool descriptions say when to call the tool.

# Brief A: Freya Bank, early-stage collections, one product

Freya Bank is fictional. Every customer, debt and payment here is synthetic.

This brief has the density of a real bank specification. Read all of it. Most failed cases come from one rule that was skipped.

## 1. The job

Freya Bank calls customers who are 1 to 45 days late on one product. The agent finds the customer, checks identity, states the debt, gets a payment promise where it can, and closes the call with the correct outcome.

## 2. Call variables

Every call starts with these. Nothing else is known before the tools are called.

| Variable | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `customer_id` | `c_4f2a...` | Pass it to every tool call. |
| `first_name`, `last_name` | `Daniel`, `Reyes` | The person to ask for. |
| `title` | `Mr` or `Ms` | Address the customer as title plus last name. |
| `now` | `2026-10-14T11:00` | The current date and time. All date rules use this, never the real clock. |

## 3. Opening and who is on the line

1. First sentence: say you are a digital assistant calling from Freya Bank, and that the call is recorded. Do not say "collections", "debt", "payment" or the product before identity is verified. This applies to everyone, including relatives.
2. Ask "Am I speaking with {title} {last_name}?".
3. Only "yes", "that's me", "speaking" or the customer's own name counts as confirmation. "Hello", "go ahead" and "who is this" do not. Ask once more. If it is still unclear after the second ask, close as `not_reached` / `unclear`. Answer a question from the customer first (rules 4 and 43). The ask that follows is the second ask.
4. If the customer asks whether you are a robot or an AI, say that you are Freya Bank's digital assistant and continue.

## 4. Someone else answers

5. Do not say why you are calling. Say nothing beyond the opening sentence of rule 1. Ask when the customer can be reached.
6. A callback is for today or the next business day, from 10:00 to 19:00, both included, and later than `now`. Call `schedule_callback` with the date and the time, then close as `not_reached` / `callback`.
7. If the person offers a day or a time outside that window, ask once for another time. If that is also outside it, do not schedule. Close as `not_reached` / `no_callback`.
8. If the person says the number does not belong to the customer, close as `not_reached` / `wrong_number`.
9. If the person says the customer has died, say "I am sorry for your loss.", ask nothing else, and close as `not_reached` / `deceased`.
10. A relative may not answer the security questions and may not be told anything about the account, even if they offer to pay.

## 5. Identity

11. Ask two security questions, one at a time: first the date of birth, then the last four digits of the phone number on file. Call `verify_identity` with the answer. Send a date of birth as `YYYY-MM-DD`, whatever way the customer said it. The service rejects anything it cannot read as a date. Read a date given only as numbers as day, then month, then year.
12. A wrong answer may be asked again. Three wrong answers in total end the check, whichever question they were on.
13. If the customer gives day and month the other way round, `verify_identity` returns `hint: "day_month_swapped"`. Ask them to say the month as a word. That retry does not count as a wrong answer.
14. After three wrong answers, do not state the debt. Tell the customer to use the mobile app or a branch. Close as `not_verified` / `failed`.
15. If the customer does not want to answer, explain once that the questions protect their account. If they still decline, close as `not_verified` / `declined`. Asking what the call is about instead of answering counts as declining. A second refusal or a second such question closes the call.

## 6. Stating the debt

16. After both questions pass, call `get_account`.
17. Say that you are calling from the collections team about a late payment. Name the product in words: "credit card ending 4821", "personal loan" or "car loan". State the past-due amount and how many days late it is.

## 7. Dates

Business days are Monday to Friday, except Freya Bank holidays: 2026-10-26, 2026-11-11, 2026-11-26, 2026-12-25, 2027-01-01.

18. The **deadline** depends on how late the customer is.

| `days_late` | Band | Deadline | Persuasion attempts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 to 7 | early | the 12th business day after today | 1 |
| 8 to 45 | late | the 7th business day after today | 2 |

19. A promise date must be today or later, a business day, and not after the deadline.
20. If the customer names a weekend day or a holiday that is not after the deadline, offer the next business day. If the named day is after the deadline, rule 23 applies.
21. If the customer gives a vague period ("next week", "end of the month", "when my salary comes"), ask once for the exact day. If they still give none, propose the deadline.
22. "Next <weekday>" means that weekday in the following calendar week. "This <weekday>" means the one in the current week. So "next Friday" said on a Friday is the Friday of the following week.
23. If the customer asks for a date after the deadline, say the latest date you can record is the deadline and offer it. If the customer refuses the deadline, treat it as a flat refusal (rule 30).

## 8. Amounts

24. Ask for the full past-due amount first. Never ask "how much can you pay?". The agent proposes every amount.
25. The **floor** is `minimum_payment` for a credit card and `instalment_amount` for a personal loan or a car loan.
26. If the customer says the full amount is too much, offer the floor, once. Say that the rest stays overdue. If the customer refuses the floor, treat it as a flat refusal (rule 30). Attempt 2 may name the floor again, on the deadline.
27. If the customer proposes an amount from the floor up to the full amount, both included, accept it. Below the floor, say it cannot be recorded and offer the floor once. If the customer does not accept the floor, treat it as a flat refusal (rule 30).

## 9. Getting the promise

28. First ask: "Can you make this payment today?".
29. A date or an amount the customer proposes is never a refusal. Handle it with sections 7 and 8.
30. A flat refusal or a non-answer uses one persuasion attempt. A no to paying today with no date and no amount is a flat refusal. Attempt 1 is for the full past-due amount, or for the floor if the customer already said the full amount is too much.
    - Attempt 1: propose the last business day of this week. If today is that day, propose the last business day of next week.
    - Attempt 2, late band only: propose the floor amount on the deadline.
31. When the attempts are used up, stop. Do not repeat an offer the customer already refused. Close as `no_promise` / `refused`.
32. If the customer mentions illness, a death in the family or job loss, say one short sentence of sympathy and make no persuasion attempt. Offer to connect them with the customer support team. If they accept, call `transfer_to_agent` with queue `support` and close as `transferred` / `support`. If they decline, close as `no_promise` / `hardship`. This rule comes before rules 30 and 41. If the customer still names a date or an amount themselves, record the promise under sections 7 and 8.
33. Never offer a discount, a waiver, an instalment plan or any term that is not in this brief.

## 10. Confirming and recording

34. Read the product, the amount and the date back and ask "Do you confirm?". Call `create_promise` only after a clear yes.
35. If the customer changes the date or the amount at this step, check the new value against sections 7 and 8 and read it back again.
36. One promise per product. A recorded promise cannot be changed or cancelled in the same call. If the customer asks, say they can change it in the mobile app.
37. Say the promise is recorded only after `create_promise` returns `ok: true`. If it fails, try once more. If it fails again, say you could not record it and close as `no_promise` / `service_error`.
38. After a recorded promise, say this sentence: "You will receive a text message confirming this promise."

## 11. Other things customers say

39. "I already paid": say that payments can take one business day to appear, take no promise, and close as `paid`.
40. "This debt is not mine" or "I never had this product": do not argue and do not take a promise. Close as `no_promise` / `dispute`. A claim that the product was closed or paid off in the past is a dispute. Rule 39 covers only a payment of this past-due amount.
41. A request for a new payment plan or lower instalments: do not describe a plan. Call `transfer_to_agent` with queue `restructuring` and close as `transferred` / `restructuring`.
42. A request for a human: ask once whether you can help first. If they insist, call `transfer_to_agent` with queue `general` and close as `transferred` / `human`.
43. "Is this a scam?": say they can verify the call by phoning Freya Bank's customer service number, and continue.
44. A question you cannot answer from the tools: say you do not have that information. Do not invent figures, dates or reasons.
45. If the customer says twice that they do not want to talk, close as `no_promise` / `refused`. Before identity is verified, the same customer is closed as `not_verified` / `declined`. Rule 42 applies before and after verification.

## 12. Closing

46. Every call ends with exactly one `close_call`, with an outcome and, where the table lists one, a reason. It is the last tool call.

| Outcome | Reason | When |
|---|---|---|
| `promise` | none | at least one promise was recorded |
| `paid` | none | rule 39 |
| `transferred` | `restructuring`, `human`, `support` | rules 41, 42, 32 |
| `no_promise` | `refused`, `hardship`, `dispute`, `service_error` | rules 31 and 45, 32, 40, 37 |
| `not_verified` | `failed`, `declined` | rules 14, 15 |
| `not_reached` | `callback`, `no_callback`, `wrong_number`, `deceased`, `unclear` | rules 6, 7, 8, 9, 3 |

If a transfer follows a recorded promise, close as `transferred` with that transfer's reason.

Brief A never uses `add_note`.

47. Thank the customer and say goodbye before `close_call`.

# Brief B: Freya Bank, up to three products

Freya Bank is fictional. Every customer, debt and payment here is synthetic.

Brief B is Brief A with a customer who can be late on up to three products. Every rule of Brief A applies unless a rule below replaces it.

## What changes

1. `get_account` returns one to three products. Each has its own `past_due`, `days_late` and floor.
2. State every late product, one sentence each, before asking for anything.
3. The band and the deadline are per product, from that product's `days_late`. Two products of the same customer can have different deadlines.
4. First ask whether the customer can pay all of them today. If not, go through the products one by one, in the order `get_account` returned them. Do not ask about today again for each product. Start each product at attempt 1 of Brief A rule 30.
5. Persuasion attempts are counted per product.
6. If the customer names one date for everything and it is after one product's deadline, record that product on its own deadline and say so in the read-back. The other products keep the date the customer named.
7. Read all promises back together and ask for one confirmation. Then call `create_promise` once per product.
8. The customer may promise some products and refuse others. For each product without a promise call `add_note` with that `product_id` and a reason: `refused`, `hardship`, `dispute`, `paid` or `service_error`. This also applies when no product gets a promise.
9. A dispute or an "already paid" claim on one product does not end the call. Note it and continue with the others.
10. A restructuring request still transfers the call (Brief A rule 41). Promises recorded before the request stay. Promises agreed but not yet recorded are not recorded. Close as `transferred` / `restructuring`. On any transfer (restructuring, support, human) add no notes at all, before or after it.
11. If one `create_promise` fails twice, keep the promises that were recorded and call `add_note` with reason `service_error` for the failed product.

## Closing

The outcome table of Brief A applies. With no promise recorded: if every product is noted `paid`, close as `paid`. Otherwise close as `no_promise` with the reason of the first product, in `get_account` order, whose note is not `paid`. With several products, `promise` wins whenever at least one promise was recorded, except rule 10 above.

# Compile a bank's policy into a dependable phone workflow

Read ALL supplied bank material and its accompanying API schema. The material is
authoritative for bank identity, opening sentences, question order, retry budgets,
business calendars, deadlines, limits, persuasion, product handling, notes, transfers,
closing codes and terminology. No rule or value may come from memory or another
bank. A later amendment overrides an earlier extract. Explicit precedence matters.
An example in documentation illustrates syntax, never the bank's policy.
Use the language, forms of address, monetary notation and date conventions of
the supplied case. Read all file types, sheet names, tables and attached flow
diagrams. The practice bank's endpoints and collection rules are not defaults
for a different case. Examples of conversations are evidence of intended
behavior; reconcile them with explicit amendments and the service contract.

Your output is JSON with these fields:

- `policy`: a compact but COMPLETE normalized specification. List source references,
  overrides and the rule priority order. Enumerate all closing combinations and
  product-note rules. Document exactly how calendar and amount rules are computed.
- `workflow`: the complete Freya workflow, using the compact syntax below for
  tools and code nodes. All prompts, routes and bank-specific logic are authored
  by you from the input material.
- `tool_config`: object keyed by bank tool name. Each value may hold `description`,
  `field_descriptions` (map from API body field name, or `path:<name>`,
  `query:<name>` or `header:<name>`, to descriptive instruction),
  `pre_process_code`, `post_process_code`, and `response_mapping`.
- `checks`: an array of local code checks. Each has `name`, `node`, optional `tool`,
  `hook` (`code`, `pre`, or `post`), `vars`, optional `config`, optional `result`,
  and `expect_vars` and/or `expect_result`/`expect_config`. Use supplied API shapes
  and fresh synthetic data. Include weekend/holiday dates, band edges, failed
  security answers, split inputs, and successful versus failed writes where code
  handles them. Do not require external calls.
- `smoke`: when the documents include synthetic test customers, provide a name,
  an initial caller `message` in the case language, and `variables` from one
  documented test customer. Optional `expected_fragments` must be short exact
  phrases explicitly required in the opening by the source policy. This runs
  just one chat turn after publication and then ends the synthetic chat. It is
  a startup check, not a full policy score. Never invent test identities. Omit
  smoke if the documents provide no usable synthetic customer variables.
- `scenarios`: when a case folder includes example conversations and usable
  synthetic test customers, turn those examples into up to 12 end-to-end checks.
  Each has `name`, `source` (document/section), `variables` (only documented call
  inputs), `prompt` (instructions to the simulated customer), and
  `success_criteria` (an independent judge's policy, outcome and honesty checks).
  The customer must answer naturally, only reveal requested security information,

The workflow is what gets evaluated. Optimize reliability across repeated runs,
not merely prompt elegance. The phone model is fixed and relatively small.

## Compact output syntax (the builder expands this deterministically)

Do NOT repeat JSON schemas, HTTP URLs, headers, handlers or fixed tool boilerplate.
The builder derives them directly from the supplied OpenAPI, preserving fields,
types, enums and requiredness. In a conversation node write for example
`"tools": ["verify_identity", "schedule_callback", "transfer_to_agent", "close_call"]`.
For an account API node write `"pre_actions": ["get_account"]`. The corresponding
tool_config entry supplies its hooks, description and response mappings; for a
pre_action its mappings are moved to the node automatically. Do not duplicate
these mappings explicitly on that node.

Every body field is baked as an unset placeholder `arg_<tool>_<field>`, except
customer_id which is baked from the call's customer_id. Never store workflow
state under one of those arg_ names. Model values arrive in config['body'] for
pre-hooks. The post-hook can remember pre-hook values stored under separate names.

A code node has `"code": "<Python source>"` instead of pre_actions. The builder
wraps it in code_exec. Keep its silent on_enter, passthrough, fallback and
transitions explicit. An end_call node can omit terminal: the builder adds a
silent end_call with message_mode=none. Deliver the required farewell before
hangup and in the order required relative to any bank closing operation.
This compact syntax changes serialization only, never policy.

Primitive OpenAPI path/query/header parameters are also derived from the schema.
For path/query parameters the builder stages model arguments in temporary body
leaves `__bank_path_<name>` and `__bank_query_<name>` (prepend another underscore
if that name collides with an actual body field). Authored pre-hooks may normalize
these leaves; header parameters are in `config['headers'][<name>]`. The builder
then removes the temporary leaves and percent-encodes the URI parameters into
the fixed contract endpoint. Do not manually rewrite its URL or method. Use
location-prefixed field_descriptions when parameter names overlap body fields.
Ordinary request-body fields retain their original names. Complex parameter
serialization is not assumed; compilation must respect supported schema types.
Automatic pre_actions have no caller-model argument turn. Supply their required
values from documented call variables or previously verified state in the
pre-hook, including staged URI parameters; test the actual unset/default inputs.

## Workflow architecture

Use compact stage-specific conversation nodes, required account lookups, code
steps for policy calculations, and terminal nodes. The following collection
patterns apply only when those actions exist in the supplied case. It is
fine for one identity node to handle name confirmation, third parties, security,
callback and pre-verification human requests. In the collection node preserve
the complete conversation history. Avoid routing on guessed user intent when a
tool result provides an authoritative transition. If the policy requires
verification before lookup, make the lookup unreachable until those checks
succeed. A failed security answer must
not be treated as success. A correction before validation is not a failed attempt.
Enforce the policy's verification and data-loading prerequisites at EVERY
account discussion/write stage, including exception/fallback routes. A code failure
must never send an unverified caller to an account conversation with empty facts.
Do not reuse a payment-write conversation as a security-answer executor. If
complete answers need deterministic validation, use a dedicated engine-run
verification step after validation, then return to a speaking security step.
Clear stale tool-result flags before each new attempt. Routes may be suppressed
until the node has spoken, so a delayed route must preserve a newly supplied
answer rather than consume it as acknowledgment of the previous tool result.

Expose only tools appropriate to the stage. Tool names, URL, fields, types,
enums and response paths must match the INPUT OpenAPI exactly. Resolve local
OpenAPI references. The phone agent calls only those endpoints. Use `default`,
not `const`. Bake customer_id from the call. For model-supplied body fields use
unique unset placeholders such as `{{arg_create_promise_amount}}`; the same
placeholder must never be a stored workflow state variable. Declare field enums
and descriptions on the body property's leaf. Do not add fictitious request fields.
Do not accidentally freeze the previous product/date/answer on node entry.

Perform the calculations the case actually requires. Calculate from the CALL's
`now`, never the server clock, for policy-defined matters such as:
business-day deadlines per product, next permissible days, persuasion offer days,
callback windows, floors and any amount rounding. Give these facts to the model
in tool responses/prompts, including actual product IDs and human product labels.
The account result is a runtime value, never a public test fixture. Code must
handle a list, JSON string or flattened keys when reading mapped data. All code
uses only json, re, datetime (and basic [REDACTED]), initializes fallback variables,
is wrapped in try/except, and has no double opening or closing braces anywhere.
An initial code node can be skipped by the chat API: prefer a conversation as the
initial node and compute callback facts within the callback hook, or include a
safe fallback from `now`. Account-derived calculations run after account lookup.
The chat API can start directly with the caller's first message without running
the initial on_enter greeting. Put the required opening in the initial node's
task_message too, conditioned on it not already having been spoken in history.
Do not assume an entry action ran merely because the initial node is active.
The builder also persists declared response_mapping values from the post-hook,
so structured lists and objects are available under your mapped variable names.
For automatic pre_actions the flattened response prefix is the NODE name, such
as lookup_response, not necessarily the tool name. Use the actual node name if
you implement a flattened fallback; test that fallback with the same prefix.

Post-hooks must remove headers and add a short `what_to_do_next` instruction to
the data actually seen by the model. Cover success AND failure. Direct it to speak
or perform the next permitted tool call immediately, never leave an empty turn.
`result` is an envelope: its `data` is the bank body; code must check types.
Post-hooks may maintain explicit state in `vars`, mapped into string route flags.
Keep tool retry budgets explicit; maxRetries=0 on writes. Do not fake a bank
success to cover an invalid request. A pre-hook may normalize representation,
but must not silently alter a customer's confirmed amount or date. Invalid
proposals must be explained and reconfirmed before a bank write. Do not rely on
raising in a hook to cancel an action (that behavior is undocumented).

Track successful promises and transfers from actual responses. Do not infer
success from an HTTP envelope alone: inspect the bank's success field. Avoid
duplicate writes. If a write failed, retry only as many times as the brief allows,
and follow its failure outcome. Never claim a failed operation was recorded.
No notes should be emitted early if the brief forbids notes on a later transfer;
defer such notes until final resolution. Pending promises are distinct from
recorded promises. A later transfer must not record unconfirmed or merely agreed
promises if the policy forbids it. Preserve valid recorded promises.

Follow the case's closing protocol exactly once. If it supplies a bank closing
operation, obey its required ordering (including making it the last bank call
when specified), and gate completion on its actual success. If there is no such
operation, do not invent one. Say required confirmations and farewell before
the silent end_call. Do not add a duplicate lifecycle close. Omit optional
closing reasons for outcomes that require none.
Prefer one authoritative closing path with deterministic outcome reconciliation
against actual recorded state and the brief. A transfer takes precedence if the
brief says so. Do not overwrite a correct unverified/third-party close code with
a generic no-promise fallback. Never disclose protected account information
outside the case's verification and privacy rules.

## Conversation robustness

Interpret the corrected portion of a sentence, not the first mentioned value.
Assemble digits spread over turns before validating. Preserve leading zeroes.
Do not validate a partial answer. Normalize spoken numbers, dates and codes
to the API's prescribed representation. Security answers must come from the
customer. Ask only for missing pieces, and retry only the failed question.
Use the supplied date interpretation rules, including weekday conventions.
An unrelated event/date in small talk is not a payment proposal.
Brief-specific refusal/clarification limits still apply to questions asked back.

Treat extraction and policy evaluation as one contract. For every extraction
field, account for every declared enum and every representation its description
permits. The evaluator must accept ordinary, unambiguous spoken entity names
and aliases using the loaded entities; do not require a caller to supply internal
IDs or repeat a complete label when the shorter name identifies one entity.
Clarify genuinely ambiguous references without inventing an entity. The
extraction model sees recent messages and its schema, not the dialogue prompt or
arbitrary workflow variables; do not assume it can infer invisible runtime IDs.
Extraction variables are shared across the workflow. Use distinct stage-specific
names for fields with different meanings or enum vocabularies; never reuse a
generic event name with incompatible identity and action-stage definitions.
Every value written by code or hooks into an extracted variable must satisfy its
declared schema too. To mark input consumed, use a declared neutral sentinel or
a separate processed-state variable; clearing an enum to an undeclared empty
string can be rejected and leave the previous value active. Check these writes
and the next turn, including out-of-vocabulary model output handled safely.

Use small primitive extraction fields with explicit neutral/unknown values. Do
not encode a complex list or object as JSON inside an extraction string and
assume its description guarantees valid serialization. Assemble correlated
statements in code from source-appropriate primitive fields. If several
statements are permitted, preserve each statement's entity, amount, date and
kind together through bounded primitive slots derived from the source, or
clarify the statements in stages without discarding the caller's other terms.
Validate representation and semantic consistency before consuming a reply.
Unknown, malformed or conflicting extraction is an explicit unresolved-input
state: clarify under source rules. It must not silently become a refusal, a
paid/disputed claim, acceptance, or a fabricated customer proposal. In
particular, a proposal classification with missing/unparseable terms cannot
consume a refusal budget merely because a parser returned an empty list.

Every speaking node must state its exact permitted questions and next actions,
derived from the source. Critical identity-field names and restrictions cannot
exist only in code or extraction descriptions: the dialogue model needs them in
its own task. Do not let it invent a plausible security question, add a new step,
or continue an earlier stage after a closing transition. If deterministic code
supplies the next utterance, make that instruction authoritative and do not
combine it with a broad invitation to improvise the workflow.
Keep entry speech separate from processing the next fresh caller reply. For
an initialized question-only stage whose complete authorized utterance is
computed by code, use on_enter {"type":"tts","text":"{{computed_speech}}"}.
Initialize that variable on every reachable entry; never speak an unresolved
placeholder or rely on an LLM entry to repeat the value exactly. Route the
next user reply to the evaluator through an ordinary deterministic transition
with condition {"operator":"always"}, omitting is_tool_call (or setting it
false), and no loop_condition that can intercept it. Documented extraction
runs before this routing. The question node must wait for the reply: it is
not passthrough. The evaluator processes the fresh fields and chooses the
next initialized speaking stage. Do not ask an LLM entry to dispatch fresh
input or choose whether the evaluator runs. Explicitly retain/consume fresh
input once across result-only re-entry and preserve caller-first behavior.
Use separate speaking stages when permitted question types differ. Reserve
LLM entry for stages whose task actually requires model action selection; a
custom prompt there must be self-contained, interpolate its actual values,
and state exact source-derived boundaries and authorized action.
A fixed TTS entry does not automatically invoke conversation tools:
preserve any source-required action after speech through an explicit, verified
engine route or a tightly specified LLM action stage. In particular, closing
must not wait for another user reply if the source requires immediate action.

Give empty, unclear, non-answer and refusal classifications explicit handling
under the SOURCE policy, including its clarification and attempt limits. A
repeated unchanged question must not bypass a source-defined termination budget.
Count questions actually delivered, including caller-first starts where no entry
speech ran. Distinguish a new reply from a tool-result-only re-entry; retain new
answers and clear consumed input exactly once. Combine initial-question rules
with exception rules rather than applying either in isolation. A new proposal
and a rejected offer remain distinct; preserve that distinction while obeying
source limits on repeated offers.

Recognize relative periods, incomplete dates and exact dates by their meaning
and the supplied date conventions, not only a short phrase whitelist. Track
clarification allowances across turns independently of the wording used. Retain
relevant prior context and resolve only what the source and call inputs support;
clarify ambiguity instead of guessing or letting a new wording reset a limit.
Handle source-language weekday names combined with ordinal or numeric day-of-month
fragments, preserving the established month/year or period context. Distinguish
an unsupported spelling from a genuinely ambiguous date; never silently replace
a resolvable customer date with a deadline just because its spelling was missed.

At confirmation, resolve corrections against the entities and terms actually
read back, not a stale negotiation index. Preserve a proposal's selected entities,
amounts and dates across clarification turns; an answer to one missing detail
must not silently narrow its scope or discard its other terms. If the reference
is ambiguous, clarify it under the source rules before changing or recording it.

Cover every policy branch: unclear name, wrong number, deceased, relative offers
to pay, invalid callbacks, suspicion/AI/human questions, refusal of identity,
wrong answers and hints, all-product opening, already-paid versus historical
dispute, hardship taking precedence over ordinary negotiation, restructuring,
partial payment, per-product attempts, ambiguous/late/nonbusiness dates,
read-back corrections, duplicate promise requests, and write failures. Only
apply a branch when the supplied policy defines it; never import its wording
or thresholds from another brief. State the full debt before asking for payment
when required. Do not introduce extra questions that prematurely solicit refusal.

Never ask the customer for an amount if policy requires agent-led offers.
Do not count a proposed date or amount as refusal where the policy distinguishes
them. Track attempts per product, respect early/late limits, avoid repeating
rejected offers. For multiple products, follow source order and read-back rules.
The user may change one element at confirmation: revalidate and confirm anew.
No extraneous internal explanations, node names, tool names or implementation
details in customer-facing dialogue. Keep questions short and sequential.

Derive adversarial local checks from the source, independently of the generated
implementation. Cover realistic extraction outputs, natural entity aliases,
unclear replies, repeated rejected offers, date paraphrases and source-defined
limits across consecutive turns. Trace complete node transitions, result hooks,
speaking re-entry and the next caller correction before encoding checks in the
supported format. Use reachable states, not invented success flags or oracle
IDs unavailable to the extractor. Include interactions between rules and the
first question, not only isolated happy paths. A deterministic replay supplied
with hand-selected extraction values validates those values only; never present
it as evidence that speech extraction or live dialogue passed.

## Platform invariants

- No nulls and no agent_config. Valid node_type, node name matches its key.
- All workflow test_variables values must be strings.
- No tools on code/api_request nodes; no pre_actions on conversation nodes.
- response_mapping on the tool for conversation tools, on the node for pre_actions.
- Mapping paths start with data.; boolean conditions accept true and True or
  preferably use explicit string state. Avoid stale success flags in retries.
- Top-level condition groups use logic=or; nest and-groups if needed.
- Every passthrough node has a final always transition and fallback target.
- Nodes holding ongoing conversation need no unconditional self-transition.
- Only the terminal handler performs hangup, after the required closing protocol.
- No context_variables dependency: the platform can silently strip it.
- No placeholder substitution inside code. Use vars directly.
- Tools must trigger actions, not merely describe them. After any result the
  phone model must either speak or call the next permitted tool.
- Stay within 4-9 nodes unless the policy truly requires more. Avoid long chains
  that delay speech. Do not expose optional workflow architecture to the customer.

Do a final adversarial policy coverage review internally before returning JSON.
